content: The physical examination of a patient with peritonitis reveals specific findings that vary depending on the stage of the disease. In advanced cases, signs of shock and septicemia may also be evident. Patient Appearance Patients with peritonitis typically appear unwell. Initially, they may seem alert, restless, and irritable. As the condition progresses, they can become apathetic and delirious. These patients are often observed lying quietly on their back with their knees flexed, as this position minimizes abdominal discomfort. They may exhibit shallow, limited intercostal breathing because any movement exacerbates their abdominal pain. Vital Signs Temperature Fever, with temperatures reaching as high as 42°C, is a hallmark of infection. Conversely, hypothermia, with temperatures as low as 35°C, is a late and ominous sign, often indicating septic shock or ongoing intra-abdominal sepsis. Hypertension may be observed if the patient has concurrent cardiac or renal conditions. Pulse Tachycardia, characterized by a rapid heart rate and weak, thready peripheral pulses, suggests a reduction in effective circulating blood volume and indicates a later stage of shock. The pulse rate may also increase due to infection or may feel diminished in volume due to dehydration. Respiration Patients often exhibit tachypnea, or rapid breathing, as a response to infection and increased metabolic demand. Skin The skin over the abdomen may appear tense due to ascites. Additional skin findings, such as spider nevi, palmar erythema, and prominent collateral veins on the abdominal wall, may indicate underlying liver disease and portal hypertension. Eyes Jaundice may be present in patients with liver cirrhosis. Periorbital puffiness can be observed in cases of renal failure. Neck Jugular venous distension may be noted in patients with heart failure that has led to ascites. Heart Signs of heart failure, such as the presence of an S3 heart sound, may be detected. Lungs Findings in the lungs may include evidence of infection or signs of fluid overload, which can occur secondary to heart failure. Neurologic Findings Neurological symptoms may arise in cases of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis or due to underlying liver or renal failure. These symptoms can include stupor, confusion, and seizures. Abdomen The abdomen is typically tense and distended due to ascites. Palpation often reveals marked tenderness. Percussion may demonstrate shifting dullness in patients with ascites, though this can be painful if infection is present. Bowel sounds are initially hypoactive but may disappear entirely as the condition worsens. In some cases, the absence of bowel sounds may be the only indication of peritonitis, necessitating a high degree of clinical suspicion. However, the absence of these findings does not rule out peritonitis. Extremities Peripheral edema, particularly in the lower extremities, is commonly seen in patients with liver disease. In some cases, the edema may extend to the abdominal wall. Patients with nephrotic syndrome or cardiac failure may present with generalized edema, also known as anasarca.
